'''''Hibbertia scandens''''', sometimes known by the common names '''snake vine''', '''climbing guinea flower''' and '''golden guinea vine''',<ref name="ANPSA">{{cite web |title=''Hibbertia scandens'' |url=https://anpsa.org.au/plant_profiles/hibbertia-scandens/ |publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia) |access-date=3 April 2023}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Dilleniaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is climber or scrambler with lance-shaped or egg-shaped leaves with the narrower end towards the base, and yellow flowers with more than thirty [[stamen]]s arranged around between three and seven [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] [[Gynoecium#Carpels|carpels]].

==Description==
''Hibbertia scandens'' is a climber or scrambler with stems {{cvt|2–5|m}} long. The leaves are lance-shaped or egg-shaped with the narrower end towards the base, {{cvt|30–80|mm}} long and {{cvt|15–25|mm}} wide, [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] and often stem-clasping with the lower surface silky-hairy. The flowers are arranged in leaf axils, each flower on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2–4|mm}} long. The [[sepal]]s are {{cvt|15–25|mm}} long and the petals are yellow, {{cvt|20–30|mm}} long with more than thirty stamens surrounding the three to seven glabrous carpels. Flowering occurs in most months and the fruit is an orange aril.<ref name="ANPSA" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |title=''Hibbertia scandens'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Hibbertia~scandens |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="Carolin">{{cite book |last1=Carolin |first1=Roger C. |last2=Tindale |first2=Mary D. |title=Flora of the Sydney region |date=1994 |publisher=Reed |location=Chatswood, NSW |isbn=0730104001 |pages=275 |edition=4th}}</ref>

Plants near the coast tend to be densely hairy with spatula-shaped leaves and have flowers with six or seven carpels, whilst those further inland are usually more or less glabrous with tapering leaves and flowers with three or four carpels.<ref name="RBGS" />

The flowers have been reported as having an unpleasant odour<ref name=EPA>{{cite web|title=Environmental Protection Agency - Queensland Government - Snake Vine (''Hibbertia scandens'') |url=http://www.derm.qld.gov.au/register/p00289aa.pdf |accessdate=2010-11-19 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110321005410/http://www.derm.qld.gov.au/register/p00289aa.pdf |archivedate=2011-03-21 }}</ref> variously described as similar to [[mothballs]]<ref name=Taree>{{cite book|title=Indigenous plants of Greater Taree|year=2010|publisher=Greater Taree City Council|page=65 |url=http://www.gtcc.nsw.gov.au/files/FP_Strategic_Environment/Indigenous_Plants_of_Greater_Taree_Version_3.pdf|accessdate=31 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120321193518/http://www.gtcc.nsw.gov.au/files/FP_Strategic_Environment/Indigenous_Plants_of_Greater_Taree_Version_3.pdf|archive-date=21 March 2012|url-status=dead|edition=third }}</ref> or animal urine<ref name=Hawkeswood/> or sweet but with "a pronounced [[faeces|faecal]] element".<ref name=Hawkeswood>{{cite journal|author=Hawksewood, Trevor J.|title=''Diphucephala benhardti'' sp. nov.(''Coleoptera: Scarabaediae:Melonthinae'') from heathlands of north-eastern New South Wales, Australia and its association with ''Hibbertia'' flowers (Dilleniaceae)|journal=Giornale Italiano di Entomologia|date=31 August 1992|pages=109–117|volume=6|url=http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/156.pdf|accessdate=15 February 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708112149/http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/156.pdf|archive-date=8 July 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Snake vine was first formally described in 1799 by German botanist [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow|Carl Willdenow]] who gave it the name ''Dillenia scandens'' in ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Dillenia scandens''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/534749 |publisher=APNI|access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="Willd.">{{cite book |last1=Willdenow |first1=Carl Ludwig |title=Species Plantarum |date=1799 |volume=2 |page=1251 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84237#page/425/mode/1up |access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref> In 1805, Swedish botanist [[Jonas Carlsson Dryander|Jonas Dryander]] transferred the species into the genus ''Hibbertia'' as ''H. scandens'' in the ''Annals of Botany''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia scandens''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/512563 |publisher=APNI|access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''scandens'') is derived from Latin, and means "climbing".<ref name="Stearn">{{cite book |author=[[William T. Stearn]] |title=Botanical Latin. History, grammar, syntax, terminology and vocabulary |date=1992 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |edition=4th|page=487}}</ref>

Three varieties of ''H. scandens'' have been described and the names are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]] but not by the [[National Herbarium of New South Wales]]:<ref name="APC" />
* ''Hibbertia scandens'' var. ''glabra'' <small> ([[Joseph Maiden|Maiden]]) [[C.T.White]]</small>;<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia scandens'' var. ''glabra''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/90814|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref>
* ''Hibbertia scandens'' var. ''oxyphylla'' <small> [[Karel Domin|Domin]]</small>;<ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia scandens'' var. ''oxyphylla''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/90832|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref>
* ''Hibbertia scandens'' <small> (Willd.) Dryand.</small> var. ''scandens''.<ref name=APC3>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia scandens'' var. ''oxyphylla''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/90842|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Hibbertia scandens'' grows on coastal sand dunes, in open forest and at rainforest margins in an area extending from [[Proserpine, Queensland|Proserpine]] in north-eastern Queensland to the far south coast of New South Wales.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="EPA" /> The species also occurs as an uncommon weed in [[Auckland]], New Zealand.<ref name="NZPCN">{{cite web |title=''Hibertia scandens'' |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/hibbertia-scandens/ |publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Netword |access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Some pollination surveys place beetles (from the [[Scarabaeidae]], [[Chrysomelidae]] and [[Curculionidae]]) as the main pollinators of ''Hibbertia scandens'', as well as ''[[Hibbertia hypericoides]]'' {{au|(DC.) Benth.}}, and other species from the Dilleniaceae family, they also place bees and flies as secondary importance (such as Keighery 1975).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Keighery |first1=G.J. |title=Pollination of ''Hibbertia hypericoides'' (Dilleniaceae) and its evolutionary significance. |journal=Journal of Natural History |date=1975 |volume=9 |pages=681–684.}}</ref><ref name=Rech>{{cite journal |last1=Rech |first1=André Rodrigo |last2=Manente-Balestieri |first2=Fatima Cristina de Lazari |last3=Absy |first3=Maria Lúcia |title=Reproductive biology of ''Davilla kunthii'' A. St-Hil. (''Dilleniaceae'') in Central Amazonia |journal=Acta Bot. Bras. |date=June 2011 |volume=25 |issue=2|pages=487–496 |doi=10.1590/S0102-33062011000200024 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
This species is common in cultivation  and adapts to a wide range of growing conditions, including where it is exposed to salt-laden winds. Although it readily grows in semi-shaded areas, it flowers best in full sun and prefers well-drained soil. As it is only hardy down to {{convert|5 |C|F|abbr=on}} it requires winter protection in temperate regions. In the United Kingdom it has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web 
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/48070/i-Hibbertia-scandens-i/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Hibbertia scandens'' | website = www.rhs.org | accessdate=6 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 48 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | website = www.rhs.org | accessdate = 6 March 2018}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
''Hibbertia scandens'' appeared on an Australian postage stamp in 1999.<ref name="ANBG">{{cite web |title=Plant: ''Hibbertia scandens'' |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/stamps/stamp-hibbertia99.html |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=15 September 2021}}</ref>
